x: Commentary on Sūrat al-Muzzammil. In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “O you who are wrapped up! Stand in prayer at night, except for a little—half of it, or a little less, or add to it—and recite the Qur’an distinctly” (73:1–4).

By “O you who are wrapped up,” exalted is His praise, He means “O you who have wrapped yourself in your garments,” that is, one covered in his clothes. He means God’s Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.
The interpreters differed about the state of being wrapped up that God described in this verse.

Some said He described him as wrapped in his clothes, as someone preparing for prayer. Qatādah said: “Wrapped in his clothes.” Another report from Qatādah says: “The one who wrapped himself in his garments.”
Others said He described him as being wrapped in prophethood and the message.
Those who said this include:

c: Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā related to us from ʿAbd al-Aʿlā, from Dāwūd, from ʿIkrimah,
m: regarding “O you who are wrapped up! Stand at night, except for a little.” He said: “You have been charged with this matter, so rise to it.” The interpretation that we consider preferable is what Qatādah said, because God follows it with “Stand at night,” which clarifies that He described him as wrapping himself in clothes for prayer. This is the more apparent of the two meanings.

x: Regarding “Stand at night, except for a little”: God Most High says to His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: O Muḥammad, stand through the night except for a little of it. “Half of it” means stand for half the night, or reduce it a little below half, “or add to it.” God gave him a choice among these amounts when He prescribed night prayer: whichever he wished, he could do. It is reported that the Messenger of God and his Companions used to pray at night much as they did during Ramadan, until this was later lightened for them.
Among those who reported it:

c: Abū Kurayb related to us from Abū Usāmah, from Misʿar, who said: Simāk al-Ḥanafī related to us:
m: I heard Ibn ʿAbbās say, “When the opening of Sūrat al-Muzzammil was revealed, they used to stand in prayer much as they did in Ramadan. Nearly a year passed between its beginning and its end.”

c: Abū Kurayb related to us from Muḥammad ibn Bishr, from Misʿar, from Simāk,
m: who heard Ibn ʿAbbās say something similar, except that he said they prayed about as they prayed in Ramadan—or like their prayer in Ramadan—and a year passed between the first part and the last.

c: Ibn Wakīʿ related to us from Zayd ibn Ḥubāb, from Mūsā ibn ʿUbaydah, who said:
m: Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥāʾ, the client of Umm Salamah, related to me from Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from ʿĀʾishah, who said: “I would set out a mat for the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, to pray on at night. People heard about it and gathered. He came out looking angry, though he was compassionate toward them, because he feared that night prayer would be made obligatory for them. He said: ‘People, undertake as much of the deeds as you can bear. God does not tire of rewarding you until you tire of acting. The best deeds are those maintained regularly.’ Then the Qur’an was revealed: ‘O you who are wrapped up! Stand at night, except for a little—half of it, or a little less, or add to it’ (73:1–3). A man would tie a rope and hang from it. They kept doing this for eight months. God, blessed and exalted, saw how they sought His good pleasure, so He showed them mercy, restored them to the obligatory prayer, and left night prayer optional.”

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us from Mihrān, from Mūsā ibn ʿUbaydah al-Ḥimyarī, from Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥāʾ, from Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from ʿĀʾishah, who said:
m: “I bought a mat for the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, and he would stand on it at night. People heard his prayer and gathered in a group. When he saw them gathering, he disliked it and feared it would be prescribed for them. He went inside looking angry. They began clearing their throats and moving about quietly until he came out to them. He said: ‘People, God, blessed and exalted, does not tire until you tire’—meaning in rewarding you—‘so undertake only what you can bear. The best deed is the one done consistently, even if little.’ The opening verses of al-Muzzammil were revealed to him. He said: ‘It was prescribed for them like an obligation, until a man would tie a rope and hang from it. When God, mighty and exalted, saw what they were taking on in seeking His countenance and pleasure, He lifted that from them. He said: “Your Lord knows that you stand in prayer nearly two-thirds of the night…” until “He knew you would not be able to keep count, so He turned to you in mercy”
r
. He returned them to the obligatory prayers and lifted the voluntary night prayer, except what they chose to offer.’”

c: ʿAlī related to me from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: regarding “Stand at night, except for a little—half of it, or a little less, or add to it, and recite the Qur’an distinctly”: God commanded His Prophet and the believers to pray at night except for a little. This was difficult for the believers, then God lightened it and showed them mercy. He later sent down, “He knows that some of you will be ill, while others travel through the land seeking God’s bounty,” through “so recite whatever is easy of it”
r
. God made things broad and, praise be to Him, did not make them restrictive.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us from Yaʿqūb al-Qummī, from Jaʿfar, from Saʿīd, who said:
m: When God, mighty and exalted, revealed “O you who are wrapped up” to His Prophet, the Prophet remained in this state for ten years, praying at night as God commanded him, and a group of his Companions prayed with him. After ten years, God revealed to him, “Your Lord knows that you stand in prayer nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, along with a group of those with you,” through “and establish the prayer.” God lightened it for them after ten years.

m: about Sūrat al-Muzzammil: “Stand at night, except for a little—half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it, and recite the Qur’an distinctly” was abrogated by the verse that says, “He knew you would not be able to keep count, so He turned to you in mercy; therefore recite as much of the Qur’an as is easy”

m: regarding “Stand at night, except for a little”: They stood for a year or two until their legs and feet swelled, then God sent down its easing at the end of the surah.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from Qays ibn Wahb, from Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said:
m: When “O you who are wrapped up” was revealed, they kept night vigil for a year until their feet and legs swelled, then “So recite whatever is easy of it” was revealed. He said: “People found relief.”

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from Jarīr,
m: the cloth seller, from al-Ḥasan, who said: “Praise be to God, voluntary worship after an obligation.”

c: Abū Kurayb related to us from Wakīʿ, from Mubārak, from al-Ḥasan, who said:
m: When the verse “O you who are wrapped up” was revealed, the Muslims prayed at night for a year. Some could manage it and some could not, until the concession was revealed.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us from Wakīʿ, from Isrāʾīl, from Simāk, from ʿIkrimah, who said:
m: I heard Ibn ʿAbbās say: When the opening of al-Muzzammil was revealed, they prayed at night much as they did in Ramadan, and about a year passed between its beginning and end.

evidence.text: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us from Yaḥyā ibn Wāḍiḥ, from al-Ḥusayn, from Yazīd, from ʿIkrimah and al-Ḥasan, who said about Sūrat al-Muzzammil: “Stand at night, except for a little—half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it, and recite the Qur’an distinctly” was abrogated by the verse that says, “He knew you would not be able to keep count, so He turned to you in mercy; therefore recite as much of the Qur’an as is easy” [73:20].

m: regarding “Recite the Qur’an distinctly.” He said: “Read it clearly.”

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid, who said:
m: “One part after another.”

m: regarding the verse: God means, “Make the Qur’an clear,” one part following another, at a measured pace.

x: Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “We are about to cast upon you a weighty word. The night vigil is more effective in controlling oneself and more upright in speech. By day you have prolonged occupation” (73:5–7).
The interpreters differed over the meaning of His words, “We are about to cast upon you a weighty word.”
Some said it means: We will cast upon you a word whose practice is weighty.
Those who said this include:

c: Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm related to me from Ibn ʿUlayyah, from Abū Rajāʾ, from al-Ḥasan,
m: regarding “We are about to cast upon you a weighty word.” He said: “Its practice is weighty.” He also said: “A man may rapidly recite a whole surah, but putting it into practice is weighty.” Qatādah said: “By God, its obligations and limits are weighty.” Another report from Qatādah says the same.

x: Others said the word itself is difficult to bear. Among them: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, that when the Prophet received revelation while riding his she-camel, she lowered her forelegs and could not move until the revelation had passed from him.

c: Yūnus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us that Ibn Zayd said
m: regarding God’s words, “We are about to cast upon you a weighty word”: “By God, it is weighty and blessed—the Qur’an. Just as it is weighty in this world, it will weigh heavily in the scales on the Day of Resurrection.” In our view, the soundest interpretation is that God described it as a weighty word: it is weighty to bear and weighty to put into practice in its limits and obligations.

x: Regarding “The night vigil is more effective in controlling oneself”: By “the night vigil,” exalted is His praise, He means the hours of the night; every hour of the night is a nasʾah.
The interpreters differed.
Some said the whole night is a nasʾah.
Those who said this include:

c: Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm related to me from Ibn ʿUlayyah, from Ḥātim ibn Abī Ṣaghīrah, who said:
m: I asked ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Mulaykah, “Will you tell me which part of the night is a nasʾah?” He replied, “You have asked the right person. I asked Ibn ʿAbbās, and he said the whole night is a nasʾah; I asked Ibn al-Zubayr, and he told me the same.” Ibn Ḥumayd related from Ḥakkām, from ʿAnbasah, from Abū Isḥāq, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding “the night vigil”: In the language of Abyssinia, when a man rises during the night they say nashaʾa, “he has risen.”

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Isrāʾīl, from Abū Isḥāq, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: nashaʾa means “he rose.” Ibn Bashshār related from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Isrāʾīl, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū Maysarah, the same explanation. Ibn Bashshār related from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Sufyān, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, who said: when a man rises at night, that is the night vigil. Hannād ibn al-Sarī related from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, from Simāk, from ʿIkrimah, who said it is the whole night. Mujāhid said that whenever you rise during the night, that is a nasʾah. He also said everything after the evening prayer is a nasʾah.

c: Yūnus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us that Ibn Zayd said:
m: “The night vigil” means praying at night; at whatever hour one rises, one has begun the night vigil. Mujāhid similarly said whichever part of the night you rise in is a nasʾah. Ibn Abī Mulaykah related that he asked Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn al-Zubayr about it, and both said the whole night is a nasʾah; when you rise to pray, that is a nasʾah. Mujāhid said it means whichever hour a person performs night prayer. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said it means the whole night. Ibn ʿAbbās also said the whole night, and Mujāhid said the whole night, when one rises to pray, is a nasʾah.

x: Others said it means what comes after the evening prayer; what comes before it is not a nasʾah.

Those who said this include: Abū Mijlaz said that what comes after the evening prayer is a nasʾah. Abū Rajāʾ said it means what comes after the later evening prayer. Al-Ḥasan was asked, while I was listening, and said: “Whatever comes after the evening prayer is a nasʾah.” Qatādah said the night vigil is what comes after the evening prayer. Abū Hilāl related from Qatādah the same: everything after the evening prayer is a nasʾah.

Regarding “it is more effective in controlling oneself”: the regional reciters differed. Most reciters of Mecca, Medina, and Kufa read waṭʾan, with fatḥah on the wāw and a still ṭāʾ. Some reciters of Basra, Mecca, and Syria read wiṭāʾan, with kasrah on the wāw and a long alif, as a verbal noun from “the tongue agrees with the heart,” meaning agreement and harmony. In our view both are established readings with sound meanings; whichever one is recited is correct. “It is more effective in controlling oneself” means that the night vigil is firmer than daytime worship and more firmly established in the heart, because night worship is more steadfast than daytime worship. Arabs say waṭiʾnā al-layla, “we trod through the night,” when traveling in it.

The interpreters who read waṭʾan gave explanations like ours, though they expressed it differently. Among them, Qatādah explained “it is more effective in controlling oneself” as “more firmly established in goodness and more retaining of what is memorized.” Another report says: “Standing in prayer at night is more firmly established in goodness.” Ibn ʿAbbās said the night vigil means their prayer at the beginning of the night; it is more effective in controlling oneself because it is more likely to help them keep count of the prayer God prescribed, since when a person sleeps he does not know when he will wake. Ibn Zayd said the one praying at night has greater composure and a more focused heart, since no needs or other distractions arise for him. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said Qur’an recitation at night is more firmly established than during the day and more in harmony with the heart. As for those who read wiṭāʾan with kasrah and a long alif, I have already explained what they meant by that reading.

Those who said this include: Mujāhid said “more in harmony” means that your heart, hearing, and sight accord with one another. Another report from him says that your hearing, sight, and heart should be in harmony. He also explained it as agreement with the recitation and a heart free for it. Ibn Abī Najīḥ said it is more likely that your hearing and sight will agree with you. Mujāhid said it is more likely that your hearing and heart will accord. He also said your hearing, sight, and heart agree with one another. Regarding “and more upright in speech”: He says, “and more correct in recitation.”
The interpreters said similarly.

c: Yaḥyā ibn Dāwūd al-Wāsiṭī related to us from Abū Usāmah, from al-Aʿmash, who said:
m: Anas recited the verse as “The night vigil is more effective in controlling oneself and more correct in speech.” Someone said to him, “Abū Ḥamzah, it is ‘more upright in speech.’” Anas replied: “‘More upright,’ ‘more correct,’ and ‘more suitable’ mean the same.” Mūsā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Masrūqī related from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd al-Ḥimānī, from al-Aʿmash, the same account: Anas recited “more correct in speech,” and answered that the terms “more upright,” “more correct,” and “more suitable” mean the same.

Qatādah said it helps one retain the recitation. Ibn Zayd said it is a more upright recitation because one is free from worldly concerns. The interpreters said similarly.

tasbīkh means loosening and fluffing cotton or wool. One says to a woman, “Fluff your cotton,” meaning loosen and expand it. Al-Akhṭal said: “They sent them scattering dust, as one scatters the fluffed cotton of a bowstring maker.” By “By day you have prolonged occupation,” God means that you have broad time during the day to attend to your needs and sleep. Here sabḥ and sabkh are close in meaning.

evidence.text: Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar used to read the word with khāʾ.

x: Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him completely. Lord of the east and the west—there is no god but Him—so take Him as your trustee. Be patient with what they say, and leave them with gracious distance” (73:8–10). God Most High says: O Muḥammad, remember the name of your Lord and call upon Him by it; “devote yourself to Him completely” means turn wholly to Him for your needs and worship, apart from all else. The expression comes from saying tabattaltu this matter, when I severed it. Mary, the daughter of ʿImrān, was called al-Batūl because she devoted herself exclusively to God. A worshipper who withdraws from worldly life and its means to worship God is also said to have devoted himself. This is the origin of the report that the Prophet forbade monastic withdrawal.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as sincerity toward God. Another report from him says: “Be sincere to Him.” Mujāhid said: “Be sincere to Him.” Another report from Mujāhid says the same; one version says “be sincere toward Him.” Abū Yaḥyā al-Makkī said: “Be sincere toward Him.” Mujāhid also explained it as directing supplication and prayer to God alone. Al-Ḥasan said: “Devote yourself wholly and strive.” Qatādah said: “Make worship and supplication sincere for Him.” Another report from Qatādah says the same. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: “Be sincere toward Him.” Ibn Zayd said: “Devote yourself to His worship.” “Devote yourself” means worship; he cited God’s words,
“When you are free, then strive, and turn your longing to your Lord”
He explained: when you finish fighting, devote yourself to worshiping God; direct your longing to your Lord.

Regarding “Lord of the east and the west”: the reciters differed. Most Medinese reciters read “Lord” in the nominative as the beginning of a new sentence, since a complete verse precedes it. Most Kufan reciters read it in the genitive, as an adjective linked back to the pronoun in “devote yourself to Him.” In our view, both are established readings, each read by learned reciters; whichever one is recited is correct. The meaning is: Lord of the people of the east and west and all creation between them.

x: Regarding “there is no god but Him”: no deity should be worshiped except God, Lord of the east and the west.
Regarding “so take Him as your trustee”: take Him as the one who manages your affairs and entrust your matters to Him.

Regarding “Be patient with what they say, and leave them with gracious distance”: God Most High says to His Prophet Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him: Be patient, Muḥammad, with what the polytheists among your people say to you and with their mistreatment. Leave them for God’s sake with a gracious separation. Gracious separation is separation for God’s sake, as in His words:

“When you see those who engage in mocking Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in another topic; and if Satan causes you to forget, then after remembering, do not sit with the wrongdoing people”
It was said that this ruling was abrogated.

Those who said this include: Qatādah said that Sūrat Barāʾah (al-Tawbah) abrogated this instruction: the Prophet was commanded to fight them until they testified that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of God, accepting nothing else from them. Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “Leave Me to deal with the deniers, those enjoying luxury, and give them respite for a little while. Indeed, We have shackles, a blazing fire, food that chokes, and a painful punishment” (73:11–13).

By “Leave Me to deal with the deniers,” God means: Leave Me, Muḥammad, to deal with those who deny My signs. “Those enjoying luxury” means those living in ease in this world. “Give them respite for a little while” means delay the punishment I have extended to them for a short time, until the appointed term is reached. It is related that only a short time passed between the revelation of this verse and Badr. ʿĀʾishah said: When this verse was revealed—“Leave Me to deal with the deniers, those enjoying luxury, and give them respite for a little while. Indeed, We have shackles and a blazing fire”—only a short time passed before the Battle of Badr.
God, mighty and exalted, said, “Leave Me to deal with the deniers, those enjoying luxury, and give them respite for a little while.”

He means: God has a claim to settle with them. Regarding “Indeed, We have shackles and a blazing fire”: God Most High says that with Him these deniers of His signs will find shackles—restraints; the singular is nikl.

The interpreters said similarly. Abū ʿAmr, reporting from ʿIkrimah, said that the “shackles” mentioned in the verse are restraints. ʿIkrimah likewise explained them as restraints. Reports from Sufyān through ʿIkrimah give the same interpretation.

c: Abū ʿUbayd al-Waṣṣābī Muḥammad ibn Ḥafṣ related to us from Ibn Ḥimyar, from al-Thawrī, from Ḥammād,
m: regarding “Indeed, We have shackles and a blazing fire.” He said: “The shackles are restraints.” Saʿīd ibn ʿAnbasah al-Rāzī said: I passed by Ibn al-Sammāk while he was preaching, and he said: I heard Sufyān al-Thawrī say: I heard Ḥammād say about God’s words, “Indeed, We have shackles”: “Black restraints from the fire of Hell.” “And a blazing fire” means a fire set aflame.

x: Regarding “and food that chokes”: He means food that catches in the eater’s throat; it neither goes down nor comes back up. Isḥāq ibn Wahb and Ibn Sinān al-Qazzāz related from Abū ʿĀṣim, from Shabīb ibn Bishr, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said this means thorns that seize the throat and neither enter nor come out. Mujāhid said it is the tree of Zaqqūm.

Regarding “and a painful punishment”: a punishment that hurts and causes pain. Abū Kurayb related from Wakīʿ, from Ḥamzah al-Zayyāt, from Ḥumrān ibn Aʿyan, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, recited, “Indeed, We have shackles and a blazing fire, and food that chokes,” and then fainted.
Interpretation of the words of God Most High: “On the day the earth and mountains convulse, and the mountains become a heap of shifting sand” (73:14).

God Most High says that for these Quraysh polytheists who trouble you, Muḥammad, We have the punishments He has described, on the day the earth and mountains convulse. Their convulsion is their shaking along with those upon them; that is the Day of Resurrection.

Regarding “and the mountains become a heap of shifting sand”: God says the mountains will become flowing, scattered sand. Mahīl is a passive form from the expression “I poured sand,” when its bottom is disturbed and the sand from above slides down over it. The Arabs use two forms: mahīl and mahyūl, just as they say makīl and makyūl.
“Your people used to think you a chief, and I think you are a chief who is aided.”
The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as flowing sand. Another report from him says the soft heap of sand keeps cascading when touched. Mujāhid said it will pour down.

Interpretation of the words of God Most High: “We have sent you a Messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent a Messenger to Pharaoh. Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger, so We seized him with a terrible seizure” (73:15–16).

God Most High says: People, We have sent you a Messenger who will testify against you, on the Day you meet Me at the Resurrection, concerning those among you who answered My call and those who refused to answer. “Just as We sent a Messenger to Pharaoh” means that We formerly sent a messenger to Pharaoh of Egypt, calling him to the truth. Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger We sent to him, “so We seized him with a terrible seizure”: We seized him with a severe punishment and destroyed him and all who were with him. The word wabīl is also used of food that is hard to digest.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid explained “a terrible seizure” as severe. Qatādah said the same. Ibn Zayd said wabīl means evil; Arabs say that evil has piled up against someone when hardship continues to befall him. He also said: God was not content merely to drown and punish Pharaoh, but caused him to remain in punishment until he is sent to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “So how will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, against a day that makes children gray-haired? The sky will split apart because of it; His promise will be fulfilled” (73:17–18).

God Most High says to those who associate partners with Him: People, how will you guard yourselves against a day that makes children gray-haired if you disbelieve in God and do not affirm Him? It is reported that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd recited it this way.

The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said: “There is no ‘how’—it means: How will you guard yourselves against a day when you have disbelieved in it and do not affirm it?” Another report from Qatādah says: “By God, no one who disbelieves in God can guard himself against that day.”

evidence.text: It is reported that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd recited it this way.

x: Regarding “a day that makes children gray-haired”: He means the Day of Resurrection. Children will turn gray on that day because of its terrible horror and distress.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk related from Ibn Masʿūd: On the Day of Resurrection, our Lord, the King, will summon Adam and say, “Adam, rise and send forth the contingent destined for the Fire.” Adam will say, “My Lord, I know only what You taught me.” God will tell him, “From every thousand, take out nine hundred and ninety-nine.” They will be driven to the Fire, blackened, chained together, and with grim faces; every infant will turn gray there. Ibn Zayd said the young will turn gray from the distress of that day. Regarding “The sky will split apart because of it”: God Most High says the sky will be weighed down by that day, cracking and splitting. Ibn ʿAbbās explained that this is the sky splitting when the Most Compassionate descends, mighty and exalted.

Mujāhid explained munfaṭirun bihi as “weighed down by it.” Al-Ḥasan said it will be weighed down and grieving on the Day of Resurrection; another report from him gives the same explanation. ʿIkrimah said it will be weighed down by it. Al-Ḥasan also described it as burdened and weighed down. Qatādah said it will be weighed down on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Zayd said this is the Day of Resurrection, the day that makes children gray-haired and the day the sky splits apart. He recited,
“When the sky is split apart”

and said all of this occurs on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the sky in that verse as being filled by it; another report says “The sky will split apart because of it” means it is filled by it, in the language of Abyssinia. The sky is masculine here because Arabs use the word as both masculine and feminine. Those who make it masculine treat it as referring to a roof, as in “the sky of the house,” meaning its roof.
It may also be masculine because the word has no distinct masculine and feminine form.
“If a people could raise the sky to him, we would reach the sky with the clouds.”

Regarding “His promise will be fulfilled”: whatever God promised to do will indeed be done, for He does not break His promise. Among what He promised is the coming of a day that will make children gray-haired. People, beware of that day, for it will surely come.
“If a people could raise the sky to him, we would reach the sky with the clouds.”

Regarding “His promise will be fulfilled”: whatever God promised to do will be done, for He does not break His promise. Among what He promised is the coming of a day that will make children gray-haired. People, beware of that day, for it will surely come.

Interpretation of the words of God Most High: “This is a reminder; so whoever wishes may take a path to his Lord. Your Lord knows that you stand in prayer nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, along with a group of those with you. God measures the night and the day. He knows that you cannot keep count of it, so He has turned to you in mercy. Recite, then, as much of the Qur’an as is easy for you. He knows that some of you will be ill, while others travel through the land seeking God’s bounty, and others fight in God’s way. So recite as much of it as is easy, establish the prayer, give the alms, lend God a good loan, and whatever good you send ahead for yourselves, you will find it with God, better and greater in reward. Seek God’s forgiveness; God is Forgiving, Merciful” (73:19–20).

“This is a reminder” means these verses, which mention the Resurrection and its terrors and what God will do to the disbelievers there, are a reminder and admonition for whoever takes heed. “Whoever wishes may take a path to his Lord” means whoever wishes may take a road to his Lord through faith in Him and obedience to Him.
The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah explained “This is a reminder” as the Qur’an, and “whoever wishes may take a path to his Lord” as doing so through obedience to God.

evidence.text: So recite as much of it as is easy, establish the prayer, give the alms, lend God a good loan, and whatever good you send ahead for yourselves, you will find it with God, better and greater in reward.

x: Regarding “Your Lord knows that you stand in prayer nearly two-thirds of the night”: God Most High says to His Prophet Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him: Your Lord knows that you pray for a period close to two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third. The reciters differed: most of Medina and Basra read “and half of it, and a third of it” in the genitive, meaning a period less than two-thirds, half, and a third; in other words, you could not manage what was prescribed, so pray less than two-thirds, half, and a third of the night. Some Meccan reciters and most Kufans read them in the accusative, meaning that you pray nearly two-thirds of the night, and also pray half or a third of it. In our view these are both established readings with sound meanings, and either is correct.

evidence.text: The reciters differed: most of Medina and Basra read “and half of it, and a third of it” in the genitive, meaning a period less than two-thirds, half, and a third; in other words, you could not manage what was prescribed, so pray less than two-thirds, half, and a third of the night.
Some Meccan reciters and most Kufans read them in the accusative, meaning that you pray nearly two-thirds of the night, and also pray half or a third of it.

x: Regarding “along with a group of those with you”: He means a group of the Messenger of God’s Companions who believed in God when night prayer was prescribed for them.
Regarding “God measures the night and the day”: God Most High measures the night and day in hours and periods.

Regarding “He knows that you cannot keep count of it”: Your Lord knows, people upon whom night prayer was prescribed, that you will not be able to sustain it. “So He has turned to you in mercy” means that when you became unable and weak, He returned to lighten the burden for you.

The interpreters said similarly. Al-Ḥasan explained “you cannot keep count of it” as “you cannot manage it.” He said the same in another report. Saʿīd likewise explained it as “you will not be able to manage it,” and Sufyān gave the same interpretation. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr related that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: “There are two qualities that no Muslim maintains without entering Paradise. They are easy, yet few people act on them: after every prayer, glorify God ten times, praise Him ten times, and magnify Him ten times.” He said: “I saw the Messenger of God count them with his hand. That is one hundred and fifty on the tongue and one thousand five hundred on the scale. When you go to bed, glorify, praise, and magnify God one hundred times.” He said: “That is one hundred on the tongue and one thousand on the scale. Who among you commits two thousand five hundred sins in a day?”

They asked, “How could we fail to keep count of them?” He replied: “Satan comes to one of you while he is praying and says, ‘Remember this, remember that,’ until he turns away, though perhaps he does not do it; and he comes to him while he is in bed and keeps lulling him until he falls asleep.” Another chain relates a similar report. Qatādah said: Night prayer had been prescribed for you, so “recite as much of the Qur’an as is easy.” Regarding “Recite, then, as much of the Qur’an as is easy”: Pray at night, reciting as much of the Qur’an as is easy for you. This is God’s easing for His servants of the obligation He had imposed with His words, “Stand at night, except for a little—half of it, or a little less.”

evidence.text: Qatādah said: Night prayer had been prescribed for you, so “recite as much of the Qur’an as is easy.”

x: Yaʿqūb related from Ibn ʿUlayyah, from Abū Rajāʾ Muḥammad, who said: I asked al-Ḥasan, “Abū Saʿīd, what do you say about someone who has memorized the entire Qur’an but does not pray with it, and performs only the obligatory prayers?” He replied, “He has made the Qur’an his pillow! May God curse that.” He said God spoke of His righteous servant:
“He possessed knowledge because of what We had taught him”
and
“You have been taught what neither you nor your forefathers knew”

I asked, “Abū Saʿīd, but God says, ‘Recite as much of the Qur’an as is easy’!” He replied, “Yes—even fifty verses.” Al-Suddī said it means one hundred verses. Al-Ḥasan said that whoever recites one hundred verses in a night will not have the Qur’an argue against him. Kaʿb said whoever recites one hundred verses in a night will be counted among the devoutly obedient. Regarding “He knows that some of you will be ill, while others travel through the land seeking God’s bounty”: Your Lord knows, believers, that some of you will become ill, weakened by illness and unable to pray at night,

evidence.text: I asked, “Abū Saʿīd, but God says, ‘Recite as much of the Qur’an as is easy’!”

x: and others will travel through the land seeking God’s bounty through trade and livelihood, which will exhaust and weaken them so they cannot pray at night. “And others fight in God’s way” means others among you struggle against the enemy, fighting in support of God’s religion. God showed you mercy, lightened the burden, and removed the obligation of night prayer. “So recite as much of it as is easy” means now that He has lightened it, recite in your night prayers as much of the Qur’an as is easy. “Of it” refers to the Qur’an.

The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said God then described qualities of the believers: some are ill, some travel seeking God’s bounty, and some fight in His way, so they should recite what is easy. Night prayer had been prescribed at the beginning of the surah. God’s Prophet and his Companions prayed for a year until their feet swelled. God kept the conclusion of the surah in heaven for twelve months, then sent down the easing at its end. Night prayer thereby became voluntary after having been obligatory. Regarding “Establish the prayer”: perform the prescribed prayers, the five prayers in each day and night. “Give the alms” means give the obligatory alms from your wealth to those entitled to them.

The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said: “Establish the prayer and give the alms” are two binding obligations; no one is excused from them, so fulfill them for God Most High. Regarding “and lend God a good loan”: spend some of your wealth in God’s way. Ibn Zayd said that a loan means voluntary spending beyond the obligatory alms.

evidence.text: “So recite as much of it as is easy” means now that He has lightened it, recite in your night prayers as much of the Qur’an as is easy.

x: Regarding “Whatever good you send ahead for yourselves, you will find it with God, better and greater in reward”: Believers, whatever charity or spending you send ahead for yourselves in this world in God’s cause, or any other good expenditure, act of obedience, prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, or other good deed, seeking what is with God, you will find it with God on the Day of Resurrection when you return to Him. It will be better for you than what you sent ahead in this world, and greater in reward—that is, its reward will be greater than if you had not sent it ahead. “Seek God’s forgiveness” means ask God to pardon your sins and overlook them. “God is Forgiving, Merciful” means He forgives the sins of His servants who repent and, in His mercy, does not punish them after their repentance. This concludes the commentary on Sūrat al-Muzzammil.

Regarding “Whatever good you send ahead for yourselves, you will find it with God, better and greater in reward”: Believers, whatever charity or spending you send ahead for yourselves in this world in God’s cause, or any other good expenditure, or act of obedience to God—prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, or any other good deed—seeking what is with God, you will find it with God on the Day of Resurrection when you return to Him. It will be better for you than what you sent ahead in this world, and greater in reward: its reward will be greater than if you had not sent it ahead. “Seek God’s forgiveness” means ask God to pardon your sins and overlook them. “God is Forgiving, Merciful” means He forgives the sins of His servants who repent and, in His mercy, does not punish them after their repentance. This concludes the commentary on Sūrat al-Muzzammil.

notes.en: Abū Yaʿlā recorded it (4022) through Abū Usāmah. Al-Suyūṭī attributed it in al-Durr al-manthūr 6/278 to Ibn Naṣr and Ibn al-Anbārī in al-Maṣāḥif. This report appeared above, 1/47. Abū Bakr al-Anbārī said some misguided people went so far as to claim that anyone who reads a Qur’anic expression with a meaning corresponding to another Qur’anic expression is correct. They cited Anas’s statement. This view should be neither entertained nor heeded: if one could recite words differing from the Qur’an’s wording merely because their meanings were close, one could replace “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” with “Thanks to the Creator, King of created beings,” and so on. The report they made the basis of this error is not sound from any scholar: it rests on al-Aʿmash’s report from Anas, which is disconnected, not continuous, and cannot be relied upon, since al-Aʿmash saw Anas but did not hear from him. See Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī 19/41–42.
